visible.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.
visible.tangentialFactors: The royal and CONTRALESA hostility documented here is voiced against 'the gays' - sexual orientation rather than gender identity - but it sets an official chiefly climate in which any queer visibility, including trans presence, is publicly repudiated by the province's most senior traditional institutions.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Interpersonal violent crime in townships is high for all travellers, and the KwaMashu study itself frames queerphobic violence within that endemic-violence context; the KZN-relevant finding is the targeting pattern and the royal/CONTRALESA climate, not the baseline crime rate.

sources.claim: University of KwaZulu-Natal (Durban) Masters criminology thesis, 2024 (Buthelezi, Ayanda Nomfundo): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minority in KwaMashu Township' — 15 queer participants purposively sampled from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, in-depth interviews; findings report significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings and examine adequacy of support/interventions and safety strategies.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

visible.summary:
Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.
visible.tangentialFactors: The NHTL campaign targets the constitutional sexual-orientation equality clause and 'same-sex marriage' - an LGBT+-broad official-climate signal rather than a trans-specific measure; its documented spill-over is onto homophobic violence generally.

sources.claim: Published letter (June 2010) from the NHTL and its Provincial Houses after meeting at Hazyview, Mpumalanga: while 'respecting' the Constitutional Court same-sex marriage judgment, 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts'; states they do not support legalisation of same-sex marriages, warns of ostracism and violence, and vows a five-year campaign against it.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (missing from cache); the underlying 2016 report documents the NHTL asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

GroundUp (6 January 2020) reports that Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead — half naked with stab wounds — near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, Mpumalanga, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019, and that on 2 January about 800 people marched in the Thembisile Hani Local Municipality in protest, organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence. The report documents a deadly anti-LGBTIQ incident and local community mobilisation inside Mpumalanga — province-level violence data this record's dossier had not retrieved.

MambaOnline (11 September 2014) reports that Mpumalanga's first LGBTI Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital Nelspruit (Mbombela) under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United', with around 1,000 participants marching from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza and a post-parade picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. Organiser Joy Kunene said police were 'visible and supportive' and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers to assist, and the march launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella group for the province's LGBTI organisations. The event is direct evidence of a public, police-supported LGBTIQ+ presence in the province's capital, tempering the record's picture of exclusively hostile local institutions.

Ridge Times (29 August 2026) reports that at the Pride Flag Tour held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about alleged discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations; participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after being sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she 'didn't fight back'. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation. The report, from the Secunda-area local press, documents current, province-specific LGBTIQ+ grievances about police treatment in Mpumalanga — the kind of enforcement-facing finding this record lacked.

visible.summary:
North West sits squarely in the former-Bantustan geography where the traditional-courts jurisdiction is most extensive following the Bantustan-era map: HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies these areas as a "separate legal system" whose adjudication of gender and sexual matters under customary law with a consent presumption against the individual constitutes the principal sub-national legal divergence in South Africa. The Act was declared invalid in Mogale (2023) but suspended and extended; the replacement Bill (TKLB) has been delayed. No province has religious criminal law; no statute criminalises a visitor's expression here.

North West is also the only province outside Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and the Western Cape to have received its own representative hate-crime prevalence study (2010; the GALA-hosted Love Not Hate review records only three quantitative studies ever attempted nationally), giving it a data-presence signal: incidents against queer people here are, historically, more likely to appear in research rather than only in the "dark figure" of unreported crime that characterises most provinces. No trans-specific incident series was found. The 2010 study covers gay and lesbian people; its relevance to a trans visitor is as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

The score is 0.04 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65), the two share the former-Bantustan customary-authority finding at similar magnitude; North West's additional 2010 data presence does not raise it above Limpopo because the study documents violence prevalence rather than institutional response capacity. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), North West sits higher because KZN adds a retrieved township queerphobia study and the Zulu king / CONTRALESA official alignment against queer people; North West has the jurisdictional risk without a comparable named-authority statement. vs. Western Cape (0.72) and Gauteng (0.71), the gap reflects metro institutional functioning versus rural customary-authority geography. The dossier's under-reporting caveat applies equally: a province with more recorded hate crime may simply have better reporting than more danger.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2010 provincial prevalence study documents hate crime against gay and lesbian people; for a trans visitor it works as a proxy for reporting culture and the volume of anti-queer violence in a traditional-authority-heavy province.

sources.claim: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

The trans community in North West province cannot access hormone replacement therapy (HRT) at any public health facility in the province and residents are forced to travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres to Soweto in Gauteng to get it, MambaOnline reported on 21 February 2023. The North West Department of Health confirmed it has no facilities providing HRT for transgender people, in its response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International with the SA Human Rights Commission. Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

MambaOnline (23 March 2016, citing the Taung Daily News) reported that 18-year-old lesbian Zinzi Manini Molema of Maphoitsile village, North West, was barred from attending school for refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home saying she must wear a skirt 'since I was a girl', and she stayed home for three weeks without attending any classes. Records a North West institution enforcing a gendered dress code against a gender-nonconforming pupil, illustrating the province's socially conservative enforcement climate.

A report entitled 'Same-sex sexuality in North-West province', released in October 2010, presented the results of a survey conducted under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology during 2009 and 2010, with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella collaborating; it surveyed 319 LGBT people from a largely rural background in one of the country's poorest and most under-populated provinces, asking about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT persons perceive their environment, and sexual abuse and discrimination. Provides the province-level 2010 survey behind this record's data-presence signal for North West.

visible.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.
visible.tangentialFactors: The cited prevalence studies measure gay and lesbian victimisation; their Gauteng density signals reporting culture and civil-society response capacity that a trans visitor would also draw on.

sources.claim: 'Hate Crimes Against Gay and Lesbian People in Gauteng: Prevalence, Consequences and Contributing Factors' - Joint Working Group research initiative conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being with the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology (authors Wells & Polders), the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in South Africa (2003/04); partner roster includes Behind the Mask, Triangle Project, GALA and the Durban Lesbian & Gay Community & Health Centre.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016): the companion review of hate crimes against LGBT people in South Africa states that only three quantitative studies have ever been done - the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape; a 2010 North West province study; and this national campaign study - and measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which MambaOnline (6 January 2025) reported had shown no progress. The province's most recent documented trans-specific hate incident on record.

The SA Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism (14 November 2025) welcomed the judgment of the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075), delivered on 10 November 2025. The court found the Department of Correctional Services engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the transgender inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, and held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, ordering the DCS to implement accommodations and enforce its own SOPs. Demonstrates an operational Gauteng court remedy, under PEPUDA, for discrimination against a trans person.

visible.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The dossier's own caveat is explicit: "high recorded rates in Paris should not be read as Paris being dangerous." Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the state actively banned assembly; Île-de-France's state response to Pride was protective if tense. Compare with PACA (0.65), which shares the metro-rate exposure but adds the Fréjus dress-code incident as a specific negative on public appearance.
visible.tangentialFactors: Recorded anti-LGBT+ crime here is predominantly homophobic — over 70% of victims are men — so the metro concentration figures describe the enforcement environment trans visitors share with LGB travellers rather than trans-specific victimisation counts.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Ordinary urban crime (pickpocketing, theft) and the density of protests and strikes in the capital region affect all travellers and do not move trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: Interior-ministry statistics service (SSMSI) Infraction rapide n°53, May 2025: 4,800 recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in France in 2024 (+5% on 2023; crimes/délicts up 14%/year since 2016); only about 4% of victims file complaints; acts concentrate in urban units over 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris — whose rate, 22 per 100,000 against the national 7, the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters; recorded victims are >70% men.

franceinfo (June 2025): Paris Pride (Marche des fierte, 28 June 2025) was classed a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry; CRS police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with police framed as separating opposing groups and extremists as the enemy. Visitor-relevant: big LGBT events in the Paris agglomeration now carry far-right counter-presence and a heavy security response.

Wikipedia (LGBTQ culture in Paris): Paris concentrates France's densest LGBTQ infrastructure - as of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, it hosts France's only officially organised gaybourhoods, and it stages the annual Paris Pride parade (La Marche des Fiertés). The article also records that Bertrand Delanoë became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002 and was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals - dated evidence that even the country's most LGBTQ-visible city carries a targeted-violence history a visitor should weigh.

Wikipedia (LGBTQ rights in France), the national framework a traveller in Île-de-France stands under: France introduced same-sex civil partnerships (PACS) in 1999 and became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage in 2013, with anti-discrimination protections on grounds of sexual orientation (1985) and gender identity (2012). Since 2017 transgender people may change their legal gender without surgery or any medical diagnosis, and in 2010 France was the first country in the world to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness. This supplies the legal baseline behind the record's national score (0.67) for travel-with-partner and documentation purposes.

visible.summary:
Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.
visible.tangentialFactors: The documented campaigns - the 2017 purge, the conscription blackmail - targeted men perceived as homosexual; trans-specific detentions in the republic are not separately tabulated in these sources, but the same unofficial-detention apparatus is what an official immigration assessment treats as likely to persecute trans people in the region.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Frequent terrorist attacks and general armed instability in the republic, cited by Western travel advisories for all visitors, are separate from trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (26 May 2017): documents the Feb 2017 Chechen police purge — men believed gay rounded up, held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured; some forcibly disappeared, others returned to families 'barely alive from beatings', captors outing them and urging honour killings. Report shows Kadyrov's denial notwithstanding that top regional officials knew. The core sourced basis for this record's extreme-risk profile.

Novaya Gazeta (11 Jan 2019, Russian): learned of renewed persecution of gay men in Chechnya — warnings circulated via VKontakte LGBT-group admins telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. Follows the paper's April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men for which no criminal case was opened. Establishes the purge reactivated within two years, not a one-off.

The Insider (4 Sep 2024): SK SOS reports Chechen security forces coercing detained gay men into military service — at least seven sent to frontlines in Ukraine, one already killed; methods began before the 21 Sep 2022 mobilisation order. In early Sep 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they'd be sent to front. Establishes detention-to-frontline blackmail as an ongoing persecution vector since 2022.

OC Media (Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation): a mass wave of unlawful detentions sweeping Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine — people detained over minor pretexts (missing insurance documents), taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, forced to sign contracts; families sometimes must recruit two 'volunteers' to free a detained relative. Complements the gay-specific coercion reports: conscription machinery as a generalised coercive tool of the Chechen security apparatus.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across this republic and the wider North Caucasus 2017–2024 (abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings); assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; notes the 2023 'extremist organisation' designation of the international LGBT+ movement exposing support/activity to 2–6 years (organising 6–10) imprisonment, with violence spreading beyond the region. The freshest official-assessment source for the record's trans-specific claim.
